units.translation: bus, of which the former was κοννῶ δ᾽ ἄταν χειμών [and the storm of ruin for your wife]: the - the wrath of Hera, the latter καὶ τότ᾽ οὐ δικαίοις [and then not with just means]: this refers to the above "τὸν πολυξενώτατον — Ὀλυμπίων [the most hospitable of the Olympians]", and the rest is interjected in between. He said "the rest" meaning the words "ἃ Ζὴν – χειμών [which Zeus – storm]". In the earlier annotation the scholiast said ἔφθασεν [it came] for φθάσει [it will come], because he did not know that εἶσι [it will go] has future meaning. As for the meters of the intercalary strophe, the first three verses ἆ Ζὴν – γαμετᾶς σᾶς [O Zeus – your wife] are anapaestic paroemiacs, but the fourth οὐρανόνικον χειμών [heaven-conquering storm] is composed of a choriamb and a dochmius with the most common choriambic clausula in almost every kind of meter.

the wrath of Hera who conquers in manliness all the gods in heaven. And so the wrath of Hera came upon us. To the above "τὸν πολυξενώτατον Ζῆνα τῶν κεκμηκότων ἱξόμεσθα [we will come to Zeus, most hospitable to the dead]" for from a harsh breath comes a storm. The rest is interjected in between.

and then not with just means: this refers to the above "τὸν πολυξενώτατον — Ὀλυμπίων [the most hospitable of the Olympians]", and the rest is interjected in between. The rest

about which see Apollonius' discussion in Bekker's Anecdota p. 576, 15, it is an interjection of one calling or exclaiming, usually placed once, but sometimes doubled, either within or outside the meter, with the first syllable naturally short, but sometimes placed as long in anapaests.
In the exclamation frequent among the tragedians ἰώ μοί μοι [io me, me], which has the measure of an antispast,
It is memorable that ἰώ [io] is placed three times in succession, but not in the same verse
where I restored ἰὼ δυσαίων σφὶν ἁ τεκοῦσα [io, unhappy for them the mother], as the meter of strophic verse 915 demands.
ἰὴ ἰὼ, διαὶ Δίκας – [ie io, through Justice –], where I restored ἰἡ ἰή [ie ie].
ἰώ [io] corrupted from ἴτώ [ito], which Bothius restored.
